**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** A Little Rice

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Taṇḍulanāḷijātaka* (Ja 5), translated as *A Little Rice*, is an early narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional narrative frame, the Buddha spoke the opening verse ("Dost ask how much a peck of rice is worth?") while dwelling at Jetavana in reference to the foolishness of the elder Udāyi, called the Dullard [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010]. In her study of narrative techniques in the collection, Naomi Appleton cites the *Taṇḍulanāḷijātaka* as an example of a common structural format wherein actions in the present story (*paccuppannavatthu*) are mirrored in the past story (*atītavatthu*), introduced with the motif that "this is not the first time" the character has acted in such a manner [Appleton 2010]. Consequently, the narrative centers primarily on the idiocy of Udāyi rather than on the Bodhisatta [Appleton 2010].

Neither curated parallels on SuttaCentral nor automated searches via DharmaNexus identify any parallel versions in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan literature, and DharmaNexus finds no internal Pali text reuse for this entry [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral lists six translations across four languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
